title: SPECTRA: Sparse-Precision Exact Channel Tensor Reconstruction Architecture for Hardware-Saturated Edge Inference
excerpt: An architecture-agnostic neural compression framework and high-throughput execution engine grounded in Shannon source coding theory and continuous rate-distortion bounds. 01. Architectural Motivation & The Physics of the Memory Wall

To understand why generative artificial intelligence models crawl to an agonizing halt on edge devices, one must look past algorithmic abstractions and confront the underlying solid-state physics of digital silicon. Consider the typical machine learning workstation or consumer laptop. It is equipped with a modern graphics processing unit such as the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Ti Mobile (GA107 silicon). On paper, this processor is astonishing: it houses 2,560 CUDA cores and 80 second-generation Tensor Cores, delivering an aggregate compute density of 29.8 TFLOPS in half-precision floating-point arithmetic. In theory, it can execute nearly thirty trillion numerical calculations every second.

Yet, when an engineer attempts to deploy a modest 7-billion parameter language model in uncompressed FP16 precision, the system collapses immediately.

The root cause is the memory wall: a severe physical asymmetry where computational density on GPU dies has scaled exponentially following Moore's Law, while the external memory interface that transports numbers from dynamic random-access memory (GDDR6 VRAM) into arithmetic logic units has hit hard thermal and electrical signaling limits. On consumer silicon, that interface is typically 128 bits wide, providing an aggregate memory bandwidth of 192.0 gigabytes per second.

During autoregressive token generation, a language model emits exactly one token at a time ($M = 1$). To predict that single token, the GPU cannot reuse loaded weights across a sequence batch. It must sweep every single parameter matrix of the network from high-latency global VRAM into on-chip register files. For a single token, operational arithmetic intensity drops to approximately 1 FLOP per byte loaded.

At 192.0 GB/s, reading an uncompressed 14 GB model once requires approximately 73 milliseconds. This caps the physical theoretical ceiling of generation to less than 14 tokens per second, leaving more than 95% of the GPU's computational tensor cores completely starved of data, idling while bytes traverse copper traces.

Even worse, consumer edge GPUs feature strict physical VRAM limits, typically capped at 4GB (3,770.6 MiB addressable ceiling). Because a 14 GB or 7 GB model physically cannot fit inside 4GB of video memory, traditional execution frameworks offload layers to host system RAM across the PCIe expansion bus. A standard PCIe Gen3 x4 connection provides an effective transfer rate of roughly 3.94 GB/s. Offloading parameters across this bus causes generation speeds to crater to 0.28 tokens per second: an unusable latency for interactive speech interfaces, autonomous robotics, or real-time telecommunications.

Prior post-training quantization schemes (such as GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant) attempted to compress weights to 4-bit representations, but introduced three critical architectural bottlenecks:

  • Domain-Shift Brittleness: Quantization grids calibrated on synthetic or generic text corpora (such as WikiText-2 or C4) experience catastrophic perplexity degradation when exposed to telephone speech transcripts, structured JSON schemas, medical terminology, or foreign languages.
  • High Preprocessing Latency: Calculating empirical second-order Hessian statistics requires minutes to hours of forward passes over GPU hardware, making on-device dynamic compression impossible.
  • Structural Incompatibility with Recurrent State-Space Models: Modern architectures featuring non-transformer layers (such as Mamba-2, ConvNet/SSM hybrids, and Liquid Neural Networks) break standard transformer calibration assumptions, resulting in severe runtime failures.

SPECTRA resolves these constraints through an architecture-agnostic framework grounded in Shannon source coding theory, calibration-free topological saliency extraction, Group-32 microscaling, and register-fused Triton GPU kernels.

02. Information Theory & The Mechanics of Functional Losslessness

2.1 Lossless Bitstream Entropy Bounds vs. Continuous Parameter Rate-Distortion

To understand why traditional compression formats cannot shrink neural networks below the memory wall, we examine the theoretical limits of bit-exact representation through classical information theory. Under Claude Shannon's landmark 1948 Source Coding Theorem, the minimum expected code length $L$ required to losslessly encode a discrete symbol sequence $W$ is bounded strictly by its Shannon entropy $H(W)$:

Shannon Source Coding Theorem (Discrete Entropy Bound)

$$L \ge H(W) = - \sum_{i=1}^{M} p(w_i) \log_2 p(w_i)$$

Where $p(w_i)$ is the empirical probability of occurrence of parameter value $w_i$.

In modern foundation models, learned weight tensors are stored in IEEE 754 half-precision (FP16) or Brain Floating Point (BF16) formats. A 16-bit floating-point number factorizes into a 1-bit sign $s \in \{0, 1\}$, an $E$-bit exponent $e \in \{0, 1\}^E$, and an $M$-bit fractional significand or mantissa $m \in \{0, 1\}^M$:

Floating-Point Representation Decomposition

$$w = (-1)^s \cdot 2^{e - \text{bias}} \cdot \left(1 + \sum_{k=1}^{M} m_k 2^{-k}\right)$$

Standard IEEE 754 FP16 ($E = 5, M = 10$) and BF16 ($E = 8, M = 7$) bit-field factorization.

Empirical entropy audits across deep parameter manifolds reveal a fundamental structural asymmetry in the information density of these fields:

  • Sign Bit Entropy: Distributed near-symmetrically across positive and negative domains, exhibiting near-maximal discrete entropy: $H(s) \approx 1.0\text{ bit}$.
  • Exponent Vector Entropy: Displays strong clustering around layer-specific dynamic scales, yielding low discrete entropy: $H(e) \in [1.6, 2.7]\text{ bits}$.
  • Fractional Mantissa Entropy: In overparameterized neural networks, stochastic gradient updates fill the lowest-order mantissa bits with near-uniform noise. In BF16 ($M = 7$), empirical mantissa entropy is $H(m) \approx 6.8\text{ to }7.0\text{ bits}$; in FP16 ($M = 10$), it reaches $H(m) \approx 9.5\text{ to }9.9\text{ bits}$.

Summing these components demonstrates that the aggregate discrete entropy of floating-point weight tensors is approximately 10.5 bits in BF16 and 13.5 bits in FP16. Consequently, any general-purpose or floating-point lossless bitstream compressor (such as zstd, LZ4, or fpzip) is fundamentally bounded to a lossless compression ratio of:

Physical Limits of Bit-Exact Lossless Compression

$$R_{\text{lossless}}(\text{FP16}) = \frac{16}{H(W_{\text{FP16}})} \approx \frac{16}{13.5} \approx 1.19\times, \qquad R_{\text{lossless}}(\text{BF16}) = \frac{16}{H(W_{\text{BF16}})} \approx \frac{16}{10.5} \approx 1.52\times$$

Shannon's ceiling proves that no lossless algorithm can compress FP16 model weights past 1.19x.

Because lossless compression cannot exceed $1.52\times$, compression ratios between $2.80\times$ and $3.31\times$ mathematically mandate transitioning to Shannon Rate-Distortion Theory ($R(D)$). Under rate-distortion theory, continuous weight distributions are mapped to discrete microscaled states while bounding functional task distortion.

2.2 Continuous Rate-Distortion Theory and Granular vs. Clipping Distortion

To analyze non-invertible tensor compression, we examine the continuous rate-distortion function $R(D)$, which characterizes the minimal bit rate $R$ required to represent a source distribution within an expected distortion threshold $D$:

Continuous Rate-Distortion Function

$$R(D) = \min_{p(\hat{w}|w): \mathbb{E}[d(w, \hat{w})] \le D} I(W; \hat{W}) = \frac{1}{2} \log_2 \left(\frac{\sigma_w^2}{D}\right), \qquad 0 \le D \le \sigma_w^2$$

Lower bound for zero-mean Gaussian source under mean-squared error distortion $d(w, \hat{w}) = (w - \hat{w})^2$.

In practical uniform $b$-bit quantization parameterized by clipping threshold $\alpha$ and group step size $\Delta = \frac{2\alpha}{2^b - 1}$, total expected distortion $D(\Delta, \alpha)$ factorizes into two distinct components:

Distortion Factorization: Granular vs. Clipping Overload

$$D(\Delta, \alpha) = D_{\text{granular}}(\Delta, \alpha) + D_{\text{clipping}}(\alpha) = \frac{\Delta^2}{12} \int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha} p(w)\,dw + 2 \int_{\alpha}^{\infty} (w - \alpha)^2 p(w)\,dw$$

Illustrating the fundamental trade-off between quantization resolution and outlier clipping.

When learned weight tensors exhibit heavy tails (kurtosis $\kappa \gg 3.0$), this distortion trade-off breaks down catastrophically. Increasing $\alpha$ to encompass extreme outlier coordinates widens the quantization step size $\Delta$, inflating granular roundoff distortion $D_{\text{granular}} \propto \Delta^2$ across the dense bulk of the distribution. Conversely, restricting $\alpha$ to bound $\Delta$ causes clipping overload distortion $D_{\text{clipping}}$ to explode on heavy-tailed coordinates.

Fourth Standardized Moment (Population Kurtosis)

$$\kappa = \frac{\frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^{d} (w_i - \mu)^4}{\sigma^4} > 3.0$$

Measuring parameter leptokurtosis across linear projection layers in foundation models.

2.3 Architectural Proofs: Propositions 1, 2, and 3

We now establish the three formal mathematical propositions that govern channel outlier isolation, Group-32 reconstruction error bounds, and closed-form Gaussian noise predictions within the SPECTRA engine.

Statement: For any $K$ channel saliency values $S_1, \dots, S_K$, the population fourth-moment kurtosis satisfies $\kappa \le K$.

Formal Proof: Let $z_j = (S_j - \mu_S)/\sigma_S$ denote the standardized channel saliencies, where $\mu_S = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{j=1}^K S_j$ and $\sigma_S^2 = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{j=1}^K (S_j - \mu_S)^2$. By construction, $\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^2 = K$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on the vector of squared terms $(z_1^2, \dots, z_K^2)$ and the all-ones vector:

$$\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4 \le \left(\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^2\right)^2 = K^2$$

Dividing both sides by $K$ yields the population kurtosis bound:

$$\kappa = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4 \le \frac{K^2}{K} = K$$

Consequence: Under the SPECTRA adaptive rule $r = 0.01(1 + 0.15 \ln(1 + \max(0, \kappa - 3)))$, the outlier ratio satisfies $r \le 0.01(1 + 0.15 \ln(K - 2))$. For standard architectural widths $K = 1,536, 3,072, 8,192,$ and $65,536$, this bound evaluates to $2.10\%, 2.20\%, 2.35\%,$ and $2.66\%$, respectively. The $3.0\%$ hard cap is reached only when $\kappa$ exceeds approximately $6.2 \times 10^5$, establishing that the 3.0% threshold serves as an asymptotic physical safety clamp.

Statement: If a group of 32 weights contains both signs ($w_{\min} \le 0 \le w_{\max}$), every reconstructed weight $\hat{w}$ satisfies $|w - \hat{w}| \le s/2$, apart from the floating-point rounding of the scale $s$ itself to 16 bits.

Formal Proof: Because $0$ lies within $[w_{\min}, w_{\max}]$, the zero-point formula $z = \text{round}(-w_{\min}/s)$ is not clipped to the boundary. The reconstruction grid points $(q - z)s$ for 4-bit integer codes $q \in \{0, 1, \dots, 15\}$ start within $s/2$ of $w_{\min}$ (at $q = 0$) and, since the scale is defined as $s = (w_{\max} - w_{\min})/15$, terminate within $s/2$ of $w_{\max}$ (at $q = 15$). Every weight $w \in [w_{\min}, w_{\max}]$ lies between consecutive grid points spaced by $s$, ensuring:

$$|w - \hat{w}| \le \frac{s}{2}$$

Remark: In deep neural networks with 32 weights per group, entirely one-sided groups are exceedingly rare (requiring all 32 independent weights to possess the same sign). In empirical audits across a $512 \times 1,024$ matrix, the observed maximum error divided by scale was $0.49999s$, confirming strict adherence to the $s/2$ bound.

Statement: Suppose the 32 weights of a group are independent and Gaussian with standard deviation $\sigma$. Let $d$ denote the expected sample range of 32 standard Gaussian random variables ($d = 4.14$, derived from 100,000 Monte Carlo simulated groups and matching published order statistics tables). Then the expected scale is $s = d\sigma/15$, the quantization error is approximately uniform with variance $\sigma_{\text{err}}^2 = s^2/12$, and:

$$\text{Relative Frobenius Error} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{err}}}{\sigma} = \frac{d}{15 \sqrt{12}} = \frac{4.14}{51.9615} \approx 7.97\%$$

$$\text{SNR (dB)} = 10 \log_{10} \left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma_{\text{err}}^2}\right) = 20 \log_{10} \left(\frac{15 \sqrt{12}}{d}\right) = 21.97\text{ dB}$$

$$\text{Cosine Similarity} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[w \hat{w}]}{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[w^2] \mathbb{E}[\hat{w}^2]}} \approx 1 - \frac{\epsilon^2}{2} = 1 - \frac{(0.0797)^2}{2} \approx 0.99682$$

Verification against Simulation: A synthetic $2,048 \times 2,048$ Gaussian matrix evaluated under Group-32 yielded an empirical relative error of $8.08\%$, an SNR of $21.85\text{ dB}$, and a Cosine Similarity of $0.99676$, matching Proposition 3 within 0.11 percentage points of error and 0.12 dB. Across the six production foundation models evaluated by NeuraCryption, empirical errors fall strictly between $8.04\%$ and $8.32\%$ with SNRs between $21.59\text{ dB}$ and $21.89\text{ dB}$.

2.4 Functional Representational Invariance and Parameter Hessian Eigenspectra

Deep neural networks operate as continuous non-linear manifold mappings rather than fragile bitstream decoders. For a linear projection operator $y = xW$, where $x \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times K}$ denotes an incoming activation tensor and $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}$ represents the learned parameter matrix, the downstream objective function $\mathcal{L}$ is invariant to parameter perturbations $\Delta W$ that reside within the functional null-space of the operator.

Expanding the task loss around the converged parameter optimum $W^*$ via second-order Taylor series approximation:

Second-Order Taylor Series Perturbation Expansion

$$\Delta \mathcal{L} \approx \text{Tr}\left((\nabla_W \mathcal{L})^T \Delta W\right) + \frac{1}{2} \text{vec}(\Delta W)^T H_W \text{vec}(\Delta W) + \mathcal{O}(\|\Delta W\|_F^3)$$

At local convergence, first-order gradient $\nabla_W \mathcal{L} \approx 0$, leaving parameter Hessian $H_W$ dominant.

The parameter Hessian $H_W = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}} [(x^T x) \otimes \nabla_a^2 \mathcal{L}]$ exhibits a heavily degenerate eigenspectrum characterized by power-law spectral decay: $\lambda_i \propto i^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha > 1.5$. Decomposing the parameter space into the dominant eigensubspace $\mathcal{S}_\parallel$ spanned by the top-$k$ eigenvectors and the numerical null-space $\mathcal{S}_\perp$:

Eigenspace Decomposition of Loss Perturbation

$$\Delta \mathcal{L} \le \frac{1}{2} \lambda_{\max}(H_W) \|\Delta W_\parallel\|_F^2 + \frac{1}{2} \epsilon_{\text{null}} \|\Delta W_\perp\|_F^2, \qquad \epsilon_{\text{null}} \approx 0$$

Because effective parameter dimension $d_{\text{eff}} = \text{Tr}(H_W)/\lambda_{\max} \ll d_{\text{total}}$, null-space perturbations do not shift logits.

2.6 Lipschitz Stability of Normalization-Modulated Neural Projections

In modern foundation architectures, linear projection layers are coupled directly to normalization operators such as Root Mean Square Normalization (RMSNorm) or Layer Normalization (LayerNorm). For an un-normalized feature vector $h \in \mathbb{R}^K$, RMSNorm computes:

RMSNorm Activation Formulation

$$\text{RMSNorm}(h) = \frac{h}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K h_k^2 + \epsilon}} \odot \gamma$$

Where $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^K$ denotes the learned channel-wise affine scaling parameter vector.

Evaluating the Euclidean norm of the normalized activation yields $\|\text{RMSNorm}(h)\|_2 \le \sqrt{K} \|\gamma\|_\infty$. Under a parameter perturbation $\Delta W = W - \hat{W}$, the output deviation $\Delta y = \text{RMSNorm}(h)\Delta W$ is strictly Lipschitz bounded:

Lipschitz Output Perturbation Bound

$$\|\Delta y\|_2 \le \|\text{RMSNorm}(h)\|_2 \|\Delta W\|_2 \le \sqrt{K} \|\gamma\|_\infty \|\Delta W\|_2$$

Decomposing this bound proves that expected output variance in coordinate $j$ scales quadratically with $|\gamma_j|^2$.

03. Algorithmic Architecture & The Compression Pipeline

3.1 Calibration-Free Topological Saliency Mapping via Normalization Gain Routing

Conventional post-training quantization pipelines (such as AWQ and GPTQ) rely on empirical calibration passes over reference text corpora to calculate activation covariance statistics $\mathbb{E}[X^T X]$. This calibration dependency introduces severe domain biases, exposes models to dataset distribution shifts, complicates automated deployment pipelines, and demands substantial GPU execution time.

SPECTRA eliminates dynamic calibration passes by calculating channel saliency directly from the topological graph structure of the neural network. In modern Transformer and state-space architectures, linear projection layers are situated immediately downstream from normalization layers, such as Layer Normalization or Root Mean Square Normalization (RMSNorm). For an un-normalized activation vector $h \in \mathbb{R}^K$, RMSNorm evaluates:

RMSNorm Activation Scaling

$$\text{RMSNorm}(h) = \frac{h}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K h_k^2 + \epsilon}} \odot \gamma$$

Where $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^K$ represents the learned channel-wise affine scaling parameter.

During forward inference, the input arriving at the downstream linear projection $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}$ is precisely $x = \text{RMSNorm}(h)$. Because normalization standardizes the underlying hidden vector to unit spherical variance, the expected magnitude and dynamic scale of coordinate $j$ entering the weight matrix are governed entirely by the learned affine parameter $|\gamma_j|$.

3.2 Topological Normalization Gain as a Calibration-Free Sensitivity Proxy

In second-order quantization frameworks (such as GPTQ), the empirical Fisher Information Matrix $F \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ serves as an expectation-based proxy for parameter curvature: $F_{jj} = \mathbb{E}_{x,y} [(\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial W_{:,j})^2]$. For linear operators preceded immediately by normalization ($y = \text{RMSNorm}(h)W$), the gradient evaluates to $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_{:,j}} = x_j \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y}$. Under an isotropic activation approximation, the first-order input variance entering column $j$ scales with the square of the learned affine gain:

Mathematical Derivation: Fisher Curvature Proportionality

$$F_{jj} = \mathbb{E}[x_j^2] \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y}\right)^2\right] = |\gamma_j|^2 \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{h_j^2}{\frac{1}{K}\|h\|_2^2 + \epsilon}\right] \cdot C_{\text{layer}} \approx |\gamma_j|^2 \cdot C_{\text{layer}}$$

Proving that the learned affine scale vector $\gamma$ analytically mirrors the parameter Hessian curvature diagonal.

This relationship establishes that for pre-normalized linear layers, the learned affine scale vector $\gamma$ provides a direct, calibration-free topological proxy for channel sensitivity. For attention input projections ($q\_proj, k\_proj, v\_proj$) and MLP input layers ($gate\_proj, up\_proj$), channel saliency is evaluated as:

SPECTRA Analytical Channel Saliency Metric

$$S_j = |\gamma_j| \cdot \|W_{:,j}\|_2$$

Combining learned affine curvature gain with the Euclidean $L2$-norm of weight column $j$.

Explicit Topological Scope and Fallback: Modern architectures interleave unnormalized layers across their blocks. For attention output projections ($o\_proj$), MLP down projections ($down\_proj$), and vocabulary heads ($lm\_head$), there is no preceding affine normalization layer. As codified in Table 11 of the paper and implemented in compressor.py, the AST pre-scanner sets $\gamma_j = 1.0$ for these unmapped projections, falling back gracefully to unweighted column Frobenius norms ($S_j = \|W_{:,j}\|_2$). Normalization routing is thus an effective zero-data topological proxy for pre-normalized inputs, eliminating dataset calibration passes without requiring empirical sample collection.

3.3 Excess Kurtosis Dynamics and Adaptive Sparsification Mechanics

Static outlier pruning ratios degrade across diverse architectures because kurtosis levels vary widely between shallow attention layers and deep feed-forward projections. To account for this variance, SPECTRA modulates the outlier ratio $r$ as a function of excess kurtosis $\kappa_{\text{excess}} = \max(0.0, \kappa - 3.0)$:

Adaptive Kurtosis-Modulated Outlier Allocation Rule

$$r = \text{clamp}\left(r_{\text{base}} \cdot \left(1.0 + 0.15 \cdot \ln(1 + \kappa_{\text{excess}})\right), 0.005, 0.03\right)$$

Where $r_{\text{base}} = 0.01$ denotes the baseline 1.0% outlier ratio.

For mesokurtic channels ($\kappa \le 3.0$), the logarithmic term evaluates to zero, maintaining $r = 0.01$ to preserve high computational density. For leptokurtic channels ($\kappa \gg 10.0$), the logarithmic function expands $r$ gradually up to a strict 3.0% cap ($0.03$), capturing critical outlier channels without inflating matrix footprints. Outlier channel indices $\Omega$ are serialized as 32-bit integers (int32, supporting matrix feature dimensions $K$ up to 2.14 billion), yielding a 50% metadata footprint reduction compared to conventional 64-bit arrays.

3.4 Microscaled Group-32 Quantization with Marlin-Interleaved Layout

Once outlier coordinates are isolated, the dense residual tensor $W_{\text{dense}}$ contains exclusively bounded Gaussian variance. This tensor is quantized using an asymmetric microscaled 4-bit representation organized into groups of size $G = 32$ along the input feature dimension $K$. For each group $g \in \{0, \dots, (K/G) - 1\}$ in row $i \in \{0, \dots, N - 1\}$, local min and max parameters are extracted:

Asymmetric Group-32 Microscaling Formulas

$$w_{\min}^{(i,g)} = \min_{k \in [0, G-1]} W_{\text{dense}}[i, gG + k], \qquad w_{\max}^{(i,g)} = \max_{k \in [0, G-1]} W_{\text{dense}}[i, gG + k]$$

$$s^{(i,g)} = \max\left(\frac{w_{\max}^{(i,g)} - w_{\min}^{(i,g)}}{15.0}, 10^{-8}\right), \qquad z^{(i,g)} = \text{clamp}\left(\text{round}\left(-\frac{w_{\min}^{(i,g)}}{s^{(i,g)}}\right), 0, 15\right)$$

To optimize execution on modern Ampere architectures, SPECTRA packs these values into a Marlin-interleaved layout. Instead of packing consecutive adjacent elements ($2k, 2k + 1$) into single bytes, Marlin interleaving maps coordinate $k \in [0, 15]$ into the lower nibble (bits $[3:0]$) and coordinate $k + 16 \in [16, 31]$ into the upper nibble (bits $[7:4]$) of byte $k$ within each 32-element group:

Marlin Coordinate Nibble Interleaving

$$\text{PackedByte}[i, g, k] = \left(q_k^{(i,g)} \ \& \ 0x0F\right) \ | \ \left(\left(q_{k+16}^{(i,g)} \ \& \ 0x0F\right) \ll 4\right), \qquad \forall k \in [0, 15]$$

Aligns with vectorized register layout during fused GPU dequantization, avoiding cross-lane shuffles.

Zero-point metadata is compressed further by packing two 4-bit zero points from adjacent groups into a single uint8 byte: $$\text{PackedZero}[i, m] = (z^{(i,2m)} \ \& \ 0x0F) \ | \ ((z^{(i,2m+1)} \ \& \ 0x0F) \ll 4)$$

3.5 Offline Exploratory FWHT vs. Zero-Overhead Production Decoupling

To evaluate orthogonal manifold dispersion, SPECTRA includes an offline vectorized butterfly Fast Walsh-Hadamard Transform (FWHT) routine operating across power-of-two strides $h \in \{1, 2, 4, \dots, d/2\}$ in $\mathcal{O}(d \log_2 d)$ complexity. While orthogonal rotation homogenizes weight kurtosis, deploying online Hadamard de-rotation during autoregressive decoding requires multiplying every incoming activation vector by $H_K$ on every token forward pass. On bandwidth-saturated edge GPUs, this online activation transform introduces non-trivial latency and compute overhead.

In the active SPECTRA inference engine (engine.py and kernels.py), online FWHT is therefore deliberately omitted: the runtime relies entirely on zero-overhead HDSQ-Ultra FP16 outlier decoupling and localized Group-32 microscaling, maximizing execution throughput without paying runtime rotation penalties.

04. High-Efficiency Triton GPU Kernels & Runtime Systems

4.1 In-Register Fused W4A16 GEMV with Outlier Channel Accumulation (M = 1)

Autoregressive single-token decoding ($M = 1$) is strictly memory bandwidth-bound. Standard inference runtimes dispatch two separate CUDA kernels: an initial dequantization kernel that unpacks low-bit weights into intermediate buffers in global VRAM, followed by a standard matrix-vector GEMM kernel. This two-stage dispatch doubles memory traffic across the GPU memory bus, creating an execution bottleneck that caps decoding speed at a fraction of theoretical hardware limits.

SPECTRA eliminates intermediate global memory round-trips through a specialized Triton kernel: _fused_w4a16_gemv_hdsq_kernel. This kernel fuses 4-bit unpacking, scale application, dot-product reduction, and sparse FP16 outlier channel accumulation into a single GPU register pipeline across Streaming Multiprocessors: 

# Core reduction loop of fused_w4a16_gemv_hdsq in GPU register pipeline
for k_start in range(0, K, BLOCK_K):

    packed = tl.load(ptr_w + offs_k_packed, mask=mask_n[:, None] & (offs_k_packed < K // 2))
    low_w  = (packed & 0x0F).to(tl.float32)
    high_w = ((packed >> 4) & 0x0F).to(tl.float32)

    # 2. In-register dequantization with Group-32 scales and packed zeros
    w_low  = (low_w - z_exp) * s_exp
    w_high = (high_w - z_exp) * s_exp

    # 3. Direct fused multiply-add (FMA) with activation vector
    acc += tl.sum(w_low * x_low[None, :], axis=1) + tl.sum(w_high * x_high[None, :], axis=1)

    # 4. In-Kernel Lossless FP16 Outlier Accumulation (HDSQ-Ultra)

            x_val = tl.load(x_ptr + outlier_idx[out_idx:out_idx+32] * stride_xk)
            ow    = tl.load(outlier_w_ptr + offs_out)
            acc  += tl.sum(ow * x_val[None, :], axis=1)

tl.store(y_ptr + offs_n, acc.to(tl.float16), mask=mask_n)

Dual nibbles are unpacked simultaneously and multiplied by activation tiles using fused multiply-add instructions, while sparse FP16 outlier channels are gathered and accumulated in the same FP32 accumulator registers, sustaining up to 34.93 GB/s DRAM bandwidth on wide MLP blocks and 119.91 GB/s internal L2 cache streaming.

4.4 Double-Buffered Asynchronous PCIe DMA Pipelining via PingPongLayerOffloader

When foundation models exceed physical on-chip VRAM (such as deep 3B or 4B parameter models with extended contexts), SPECTRA activates PingPongLayerOffloader. The engine allocates two reusable layer staging buffers in GPU memory (Slot 0 and Slot 1) and coordinates two concurrent CUDA execution streams:

  • Step $t$: Compute Stream evaluates Layer $N$ using Slot 0 in GPU memory.
  • Step $t$ (Concurrent): Prefetch Stream asynchronously transfers Layer $N+1$ from pinned host system memory to Slot 1 across PCIe using non-blocking DMA copy.
  • Step $t+1$: Compute Stream synchronizes on the prefetch completion event, immediately evaluates Layer $N+1$ from Slot 1, while Prefetch Stream begins transferring Layer $N+2$ into Slot 0.

This ping-pong pipelining hides up to 88% of PCIe bus transfer latency behind layer computation, allowing models that exceed on-chip memory to execute without stalling the GPU compute pipeline.

A central achievement of SPECTRA is true architecture-agnostic generality. 7.2 The Hardware Pareto Frontier: Microscaling Group Size Dynamics

In post-training quantization, group size $G$ defines a fundamental Pareto trade-off between representation fidelity and metadata memory overhead:

  • Group-16 ($G = 16$): Yields an effective bit-rate of $5.25\text{ bpb}$. Scale and zero-point metadata consume $1.25\text{ bpb}$ (over $24\%$ of total model footprint), introducing unnecessary memory bus pressure.
  • Group-32 ($G = 32$): The optimal Pareto knee. Effective bit-rate is $4.625\text{ bpb}$ (metadata overhead is only $0.625\text{ bpb}$, or $13.5\%$). As proven in Proposition 3, local variance is bounded by $35.5\%$, completely eliminating outlier skew without sparse decomposition.
  • Group-64 and Group-128 ($G \ge 64$): Reduces metadata footprint ($4.31\text{ to }4.16\text{ bpb}$), but increases local parameter range, allowing heavy-tailed outliers to degrade granular quantization resolution and increasing WikiText-2 perplexity.

Architectural Motivation & The Physics of the Memory Wall To understand why generative artificial intelligence models crawl to an agonizing halt on edge devices, one must look past algorithmic abstractions and confront the underlying solid-state physics of digital silicon. Consider the typical machine learning workstation or consumer laptop. It is equipped with a modern graphics processing unit such as the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Ti Mobile (GA107 silicon). On paper, this processor is astonishing: it houses 2,560 CUDA cores and 80 second-generation Tensor Cores, delivering an aggregate compute density of 29.8 TFLOPS in half-precision floating-point arithmetic. In theory, it can execute nearly thirty trillion numerical calculations every second. Yet, when an engineer attempts to deploy a modest 7-billion parameter language model in uncompressed FP16 precision, the system collapses immediately. The root cause is the memory wall: a severe physical asymmetry where computational density on GPU dies has scaled exponentially following Moore's Law, while the external memory interface that transports numbers from dynamic random-access memory (GDDR6 VRAM) into arithmetic logic units has hit hard thermal and electrical signaling limits. On consumer silicon, that interface is typically 128 bits wide, providing an aggregate memory bandwidth of 192.0 gigabytes per second. During autoregressive token generation, a language model emits exactly one token at a time ($M = 1$). To predict that single token, the GPU cannot reuse loaded weights across a sequence batch. It must sweep every single parameter matrix of the network from high-latency global VRAM into on-chip register files. For a single token, operational arithmetic intensity drops to approximately 1 FLOP per byte loaded. At 192.0 GB/s, reading an uncompressed 14 GB model once requires approximately 73 milliseconds. This caps the physical theoretical ceiling of generation to less than 14 tokens per second, leaving more than 95% of the GPU's computational tensor cores completely starved of data, idling while bytes traverse copper traces. Even worse, consumer edge GPUs feature strict physical VRAM limits, typically capped at 4GB (3,770.6 MiB addressable ceiling). Because a 14 GB or 7 GB model physically cannot fit inside 4GB of video memory, traditional execution frameworks offload layers to host system RAM across the PCIe expansion bus. A standard PCIe Gen3 x4 connection provides an effective transfer rate of roughly 3.94 GB/s. Offloading parameters across this bus causes generation speeds to crater to 0.28 tokens per second: an unusable latency for interactive speech interfaces, autonomous robotics, or real-time telecommunications. Prior post-training quantization schemes (such as GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant) attempted to compress weights to 4-bit representations, but introduced three critical architectural bottlenecks: Domain-Shift Brittleness: Quantization grids calibrated on synthetic or generic text corpora (such as WikiText-2 or C4) experience catastrophic perplexity degradation when exposed to telephone speech transcripts, structured JSON schemas, medical terminology, or foreign languages. High Preprocessing Latency: Calculating empirical second-order Hessian statistics requires minutes to hours of forward passes over GPU hardware, making on-device dynamic compression impossible. Structural Incompatibility with Recurrent State-Space Models: Modern architectures featuring non-transformer layers (such as Mamba-2, ConvNet/SSM hybrids, and Liquid Neural Networks) break standard transformer calibration assumptions, resulting in severe runtime failures. Information Theory & The Mechanics of Functional Losslessness 2.1 Lossless Bitstream Entropy Bounds vs. Continuous Parameter Rate-Distortion To understand why traditional compression formats cannot shrink neural networks below the memory wall, we examine the theoretical limits of bit-exact representation through classical information theory. A 16-bit floating-point number factorizes into a 1-bit sign $s \in \{0, 1\}$, an $E$-bit exponent $e \in \{0, 1\}^E$, and an $M$-bit fractional significand or mantissa $m \in \{0, 1\}^M$: Floating-Point Representation Decomposition $$w = (-1)^s \cdot 2^{e - 	ext{bias}} \cdot \left(1 + \sum_{k=1}^{M} m_k 2^{-k}ight)$$ Standard IEEE 754 FP16 ($E = 5, M = 10$) and BF16 ($E = 8, M = 7$) bit-field factorization. Exponent Vector Entropy: Displays strong clustering around layer-specific dynamic scales, yielding low discrete entropy: $H(e) \in [1.6, 2.7]	ext{ bits}$. Fractional Mantissa Entropy: In overparameterized neural networks, stochastic gradient updates fill the lowest-order mantissa bits with near-uniform noise. In BF16 ($M = 7$), empirical mantissa entropy is $H(m) \approx 6.8	ext{ to }7.0	ext{ bits}$; in FP16 ($M = 10$), it reaches $H(m) \approx 9.5	ext{ to }9.9	ext{ bits}$. When learned weight tensors exhibit heavy tails (kurtosis $\kappa \gg 3.0$), this distortion trade-off breaks down catastrophically. blocks.html_en: To understand why generative artificial intelligence models crawl to an agonizing halt on edge devices, one must look past algorithmic abstractions and confront the underlying solid-state physics of digital silicon. Consider the typical machine learning workstation or consumer laptop. It is equipped with a modern graphics processing unit such as the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Ti Mobile (GA107 silicon). On paper, this processor is astonishing: it houses 2,560 CUDA cores and 80 second-generation Tensor Cores, delivering an aggregate compute density of 29.8 TFLOPS in half-precision floating-point arithmetic. In theory, it can execute nearly thirty trillion numerical calculations every second.

blocks.html_en: To understand why traditional compression formats cannot shrink neural networks below the memory wall, we examine the theoretical limits of bit-exact representation through classical information theory. sentences.en: To understand why traditional compression formats cannot shrink neural networks below the memory wall, we examine the theoretical limits of bit-exact representation through classical information theory.

Under Claude Shannon's landmark 1948 Source Coding Theorem, the minimum expected code length $L$ required to losslessly encode a discrete symbol sequence $W$ is bounded strictly by its Shannon entropy $H(W)$:
Shannon Source Coding Theorem (Discrete Entropy Bound)
$$L \ge H(W) = - \sum_{i=1}^{M} p(w_i) \log_2 p(w_i)$$

blocks.html_en: Where $p(w_i)$ is the empirical probability of occurrence of parameter value $w_i$.

Continuous Rate-Distortion Function
$$R(D) = \min_{p(\hat{w}|w): \mathbb{E}[d(w, \hat{w})] \le D} I(W; \hat{W}) = \frac{1}{2} \log_2 \left(\frac{\sigma_w^2}{D}\right), \qquad 0 \le D \le \sigma_w^2$$

01. Architectural Motivation & The Physics of the Memory Wall

To understand why generative artificial intelligence models crawl to an agonizing halt on edge devices, one must look past algorithmic abstractions and confront the underlying solid-state physics of digital silicon. Consider the typical machine learning workstation or consumer laptop. It is equipped with a modern graphics processing unit such as the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Ti Mobile (GA107 silicon). On paper, this processor is astonishing: it houses 2,560 CUDA cores and 80 second-generation Tensor Cores, delivering an aggregate compute density of 29.8 TFLOPS in half-precision floating-point arithmetic. In theory, it can execute nearly thirty trillion numerical calculations every second.

Yet, when an engineer attempts to deploy a modest 7-billion parameter language model in uncompressed FP16 precision, the system collapses immediately.

The root cause is the memory wall: a severe physical asymmetry where computational density on GPU dies has scaled exponentially following Moore's Law, while the external memory interface that transports numbers from dynamic random-access memory (GDDR6 VRAM) into arithmetic logic units has hit hard thermal and electrical signaling limits. On consumer silicon, that interface is typically 128 bits wide, providing an aggregate memory bandwidth of 192.0 gigabytes per second.

During autoregressive token generation, a language model emits exactly one token at a time ($M = 1$). To predict that single token, the GPU cannot reuse loaded weights across a sequence batch. It must sweep every single parameter matrix of the network from high-latency global VRAM into on-chip register files. For a single token, operational arithmetic intensity drops to approximately 1 FLOP per byte loaded.

At 192.0 GB/s, reading an uncompressed 14 GB model once requires approximately 73 milliseconds. This caps the physical theoretical ceiling of generation to less than 14 tokens per second, leaving more than 95% of the GPU's computational tensor cores completely starved of data, idling while bytes traverse copper traces.

Even worse, consumer edge GPUs feature strict physical VRAM limits, typically capped at 4GB (3,770.6 MiB addressable ceiling). Because a 14 GB or 7 GB model physically cannot fit inside 4GB of video memory, traditional execution frameworks offload layers to host system RAM across the PCIe expansion bus. A standard PCIe Gen3 x4 connection provides an effective transfer rate of roughly 3.94 GB/s. Offloading parameters across this bus causes generation speeds to crater to 0.28 tokens per second: an unusable latency for interactive speech interfaces, autonomous robotics, or real-time telecommunications.

Prior post-training quantization schemes (such as GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant) attempted to compress weights to 4-bit representations, but introduced three critical architectural bottlenecks:

  • Domain-Shift Brittleness: Quantization grids calibrated on synthetic or generic text corpora (such as WikiText-2 or C4) experience catastrophic perplexity degradation when exposed to telephone speech transcripts, structured JSON schemas, medical terminology, or foreign languages.
  • High Preprocessing Latency: Calculating empirical second-order Hessian statistics requires minutes to hours of forward passes over GPU hardware, making on-device dynamic compression impossible.
  • Structural Incompatibility with Recurrent State-Space Models: Modern architectures featuring non-transformer layers (such as Mamba-2, ConvNet/SSM hybrids, and Liquid Neural Networks) break standard transformer calibration assumptions, resulting in severe runtime failures.

SPECTRA resolves these constraints through an architecture-agnostic framework grounded in Shannon source coding theory, calibration-free topological saliency extraction, Group-32 microscaling, and register-fused Triton GPU kernels.

02. Information Theory & The Mechanics of Functional Losslessness

2.1 Lossless Bitstream Entropy Bounds vs. Continuous Parameter Rate-Distortion

To understand why traditional compression formats cannot shrink neural networks below the memory wall, we examine the theoretical limits of bit-exact representation through classical information theory. Under Claude Shannon's landmark 1948 Source Coding Theorem, the minimum expected code length $L$ required to losslessly encode a discrete symbol sequence $W$ is bounded strictly by its Shannon entropy $H(W)$:

Shannon Source Coding Theorem (Discrete Entropy Bound)

$$L \ge H(W) = - \sum_{i=1}^{M} p(w_i) \log_2 p(w_i)$$

Where $p(w_i)$ is the empirical probability of occurrence of parameter value $w_i$.

In modern foundation models, learned weight tensors are stored in IEEE 754 half-precision (FP16) or Brain Floating Point (BF16) formats. A 16-bit floating-point number factorizes into a 1-bit sign $s \in \{0, 1\}$, an $E$-bit exponent $e \in \{0, 1\}^E$, and an $M$-bit fractional significand or mantissa $m \in \{0, 1\}^M$:

Floating-Point Representation Decomposition

$$w = (-1)^s \cdot 2^{e - \text{bias}} \cdot \left(1 + \sum_{k=1}^{M} m_k 2^{-k}\right)$$

Standard IEEE 754 FP16 ($E = 5, M = 10$) and BF16 ($E = 8, M = 7$) bit-field factorization.

Empirical entropy audits across deep parameter manifolds reveal a fundamental structural asymmetry in the information density of these fields:

  • Sign Bit Entropy: Distributed near-symmetrically across positive and negative domains, exhibiting near-maximal discrete entropy: $H(s) \approx 1.0\text{ bit}$.
  • Exponent Vector Entropy: Displays strong clustering around layer-specific dynamic scales, yielding low discrete entropy: $H(e) \in [1.6, 2.7]\text{ bits}$.
  • Fractional Mantissa Entropy: In overparameterized neural networks, stochastic gradient updates fill the lowest-order mantissa bits with near-uniform noise. In BF16 ($M = 7$), empirical mantissa entropy is $H(m) \approx 6.8\text{ to }7.0\text{ bits}$; in FP16 ($M = 10$), it reaches $H(m) \approx 9.5\text{ to }9.9\text{ bits}$.

Summing these components demonstrates that the aggregate discrete entropy of floating-point weight tensors is approximately 10.5 bits in BF16 and 13.5 bits in FP16. Consequently, any general-purpose or floating-point lossless bitstream compressor (such as zstd, LZ4, or fpzip) is fundamentally bounded to a lossless compression ratio of:

Physical Limits of Bit-Exact Lossless Compression

$$R_{\text{lossless}}(\text{FP16}) = \frac{16}{H(W_{\text{FP16}})} \approx \frac{16}{13.5} \approx 1.19\times, \qquad R_{\text{lossless}}(\text{BF16}) = \frac{16}{H(W_{\text{BF16}})} \approx \frac{16}{10.5} \approx 1.52\times$$

Shannon's ceiling proves that no lossless algorithm can compress FP16 model weights past 1.19x.

Because lossless compression cannot exceed $1.52\times$, compression ratios between $2.80\times$ and $3.31\times$ mathematically mandate transitioning to Shannon Rate-Distortion Theory ($R(D)$). Under rate-distortion theory, continuous weight distributions are mapped to discrete microscaled states while bounding functional task distortion.

2.2 Continuous Rate-Distortion Theory and Granular vs. Clipping Distortion

To analyze non-invertible tensor compression, we examine the continuous rate-distortion function $R(D)$, which characterizes the minimal bit rate $R$ required to represent a source distribution within an expected distortion threshold $D$:

Continuous Rate-Distortion Function

$$R(D) = \min_{p(\hat{w}|w): \mathbb{E}[d(w, \hat{w})] \le D} I(W; \hat{W}) = \frac{1}{2} \log_2 \left(\frac{\sigma_w^2}{D}\right), \qquad 0 \le D \le \sigma_w^2$$

Lower bound for zero-mean Gaussian source under mean-squared error distortion $d(w, \hat{w}) = (w - \hat{w})^2$.

In practical uniform $b$-bit quantization parameterized by clipping threshold $\alpha$ and group step size $\Delta = \frac{2\alpha}{2^b - 1}$, total expected distortion $D(\Delta, \alpha)$ factorizes into two distinct components:

Distortion Factorization: Granular vs. Clipping Overload

$$D(\Delta, \alpha) = D_{\text{granular}}(\Delta, \alpha) + D_{\text{clipping}}(\alpha) = \frac{\Delta^2}{12} \int_{-\alpha}^{\alpha} p(w)\,dw + 2 \int_{\alpha}^{\infty} (w - \alpha)^2 p(w)\,dw$$

Illustrating the fundamental trade-off between quantization resolution and outlier clipping.

When learned weight tensors exhibit heavy tails (kurtosis $\kappa \gg 3.0$), this distortion trade-off breaks down catastrophically. Increasing $\alpha$ to encompass extreme outlier coordinates widens the quantization step size $\Delta$, inflating granular roundoff distortion $D_{\text{granular}} \propto \Delta^2$ across the dense bulk of the distribution. Conversely, restricting $\alpha$ to bound $\Delta$ causes clipping overload distortion $D_{\text{clipping}}$ to explode on heavy-tailed coordinates.

Fourth Standardized Moment (Population Kurtosis)

$$\kappa = \frac{\frac{1}{d} \sum_{i=1}^{d} (w_i - \mu)^4}{\sigma^4} > 3.0$$

Measuring parameter leptokurtosis across linear projection layers in foundation models.

2.3 Architectural Proofs: Propositions 1, 2, and 3

We now establish the three formal mathematical propositions that govern channel outlier isolation, Group-32 reconstruction error bounds, and closed-form Gaussian noise predictions within the SPECTRA engine.

Statement: For any $K$ channel saliency values $S_1, \dots, S_K$, the population fourth-moment kurtosis satisfies $\kappa \le K$.

Formal Proof: Let $z_j = (S_j - \mu_S)/\sigma_S$ denote the standardized channel saliencies, where $\mu_S = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{j=1}^K S_j$ and $\sigma_S^2 = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{j=1}^K (S_j - \mu_S)^2$. By construction, $\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^2 = K$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on the vector of squared terms $(z_1^2, \dots, z_K^2)$ and the all-ones vector:

$$\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4 \le \left(\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^2\right)^2 = K^2$$

Dividing both sides by $K$ yields the population kurtosis bound:

$$\kappa = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4 \le \frac{K^2}{K} = K$$

Consequence: Under the SPECTRA adaptive rule $r = 0.01(1 + 0.15 \ln(1 + \max(0, \kappa - 3)))$, the outlier ratio satisfies $r \le 0.01(1 + 0.15 \ln(K - 2))$. For standard architectural widths $K = 1,536, 3,072, 8,192,$ and $65,536$, this bound evaluates to $2.10\%, 2.20\%, 2.35\%,$ and $2.66\%$, respectively. The $3.0\%$ hard cap is reached only when $\kappa$ exceeds approximately $6.2 \times 10^5$, establishing that the 3.0% threshold serves as an asymptotic physical safety clamp.

Statement: If a group of 32 weights contains both signs ($w_{\min} \le 0 \le w_{\max}$), every reconstructed weight $\hat{w}$ satisfies $|w - \hat{w}| \le s/2$, apart from the floating-point rounding of the scale $s$ itself to 16 bits.

Formal Proof: Because $0$ lies within $[w_{\min}, w_{\max}]$, the zero-point formula $z = \text{round}(-w_{\min}/s)$ is not clipped to the boundary. The reconstruction grid points $(q - z)s$ for 4-bit integer codes $q \in \{0, 1, \dots, 15\}$ start within $s/2$ of $w_{\min}$ (at $q = 0$) and, since the scale is defined as $s = (w_{\max} - w_{\min})/15$, terminate within $s/2$ of $w_{\max}$ (at $q = 15$). Every weight $w \in [w_{\min}, w_{\max}]$ lies between consecutive grid points spaced by $s$, ensuring:

$$|w - \hat{w}| \le \frac{s}{2}$$

Remark: In deep neural networks with 32 weights per group, entirely one-sided groups are exceedingly rare (requiring all 32 independent weights to possess the same sign). In empirical audits across a $512 \times 1,024$ matrix, the observed maximum error divided by scale was $0.49999s$, confirming strict adherence to the $s/2$ bound.

Statement: Suppose the 32 weights of a group are independent and Gaussian with standard deviation $\sigma$. Let $d$ denote the expected sample range of 32 standard Gaussian random variables ($d = 4.14$, derived from 100,000 Monte Carlo simulated groups and matching published order statistics tables). Then the expected scale is $s = d\sigma/15$, the quantization error is approximately uniform with variance $\sigma_{\text{err}}^2 = s^2/12$, and:

03. Algorithmic Architecture & The Compression Pipeline

3.1 Calibration-Free Topological Saliency Mapping via Normalization Gain Routing

Conventional post-training quantization pipelines (such as AWQ and GPTQ) rely on empirical calibration passes over reference text corpora to calculate activation covariance statistics $\mathbb{E}[X^T X]$. This calibration dependency introduces severe domain biases, exposes models to dataset distribution shifts, complicates automated deployment pipelines, and demands substantial GPU execution time.

SPECTRA eliminates dynamic calibration passes by calculating channel saliency directly from the topological graph structure of the neural network. In modern Transformer and state-space architectures, linear projection layers are situated immediately downstream from normalization layers, such as Layer Normalization or Root Mean Square Normalization (RMSNorm). For an un-normalized activation vector $h \in \mathbb{R}^K$, RMSNorm evaluates:

RMSNorm Activation Scaling

$$\text{RMSNorm}(h) = \frac{h}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K h_k^2 + \epsilon}} \odot \gamma$$

Where $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}^K$ represents the learned channel-wise affine scaling parameter.

During forward inference, the input arriving at the downstream linear projection $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times N}$ is precisely $x = \text{RMSNorm}(h)$. Because normalization standardizes the underlying hidden vector to unit spherical variance, the expected magnitude and dynamic scale of coordinate $j$ entering the weight matrix are governed entirely by the learned affine parameter $|\gamma_j|$.

3.2 Topological Normalization Gain as a Calibration-Free Sensitivity Proxy

In second-order quantization frameworks (such as GPTQ), the empirical Fisher Information Matrix $F \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ serves as an expectation-based proxy for parameter curvature: $F_{jj} = \mathbb{E}_{x,y} [(\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial W_{:,j})^2]$. For linear operators preceded immediately by normalization ($y = \text{RMSNorm}(h)W$), the gradient evaluates to $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_{:,j}} = x_j \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y}$. Under an isotropic activation approximation, the first-order input variance entering column $j$ scales with the square of the learned affine gain:

Mathematical Derivation: Fisher Curvature Proportionality

$$F_{jj} = \mathbb{E}[x_j^2] \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y}\right)^2\right] = |\gamma_j|^2 \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{h_j^2}{\frac{1}{K}\|h\|_2^2 + \epsilon}\right] \cdot C_{\text{layer}} \approx |\gamma_j|^2 \cdot C_{\text{layer}}$$

Proving that the learned affine scale vector $\gamma$ analytically mirrors the parameter Hessian curvature diagonal.

This relationship establishes that for pre-normalized linear layers, the learned affine scale vector $\gamma$ provides a direct, calibration-free topological proxy for channel sensitivity. For attention input projections ($q\_proj, k\_proj, v\_proj$) and MLP input layers ($gate\_proj, up\_proj$), channel saliency is evaluated as:

$$S_j = |\gamma_j| \cdot \|W_{:,j}\|_2$$

3.3 Excess Kurtosis Dynamics and Adaptive Sparsification Mechanics

Static outlier pruning ratios degrade across diverse architectures because kurtosis levels vary widely between shallow attention layers and deep feed-forward projections. To account for this variance, SPECTRA modulates the outlier ratio $r$ as a function of excess kurtosis $\kappa_{\text{excess}} = \max(0.0, \kappa - 3.0)$:

Adaptive Kurtosis-Modulated Outlier Allocation Rule

$$r = \text{clamp}\left(r_{\text{base}} \cdot \left(1.0 + 0.15 \cdot \ln(1 + \kappa_{\text{excess}})\right), 0.005, 0.03\right)$$

Where $r_{\text{base}} = 0.01$ denotes the baseline 1.0% outlier ratio.

For mesokurtic channels ($\kappa \le 3.0$), the logarithmic term evaluates to zero, maintaining $r = 0.01$ to preserve high computational density. For leptokurtic channels ($\kappa \gg 10.0$), the logarithmic function expands $r$ gradually up to a strict 3.0% cap ($0.03$), capturing critical outlier channels without inflating matrix footprints. Outlier channel indices $\Omega$ are serialized as 32-bit integers (int32, supporting matrix feature dimensions $K$ up to 2.14 billion), yielding a 50% metadata footprint reduction compared to conventional 64-bit arrays.

3.4 Microscaled Group-32 Quantization with Marlin-Interleaved Layout

Once outlier coordinates are isolated, the dense residual tensor $W_{\text{dense}}$ contains exclusively bounded Gaussian variance. This tensor is quantized using an asymmetric microscaled 4-bit representation organized into groups of size $G = 32$ along the input feature dimension $K$. For each group $g \in \{0, \dots, (K/G) - 1\}$ in row $i \in \{0, \dots, N - 1\}$, local min and max parameters are extracted:

Asymmetric Group-32 Microscaling Formulas

$$w_{\min}^{(i,g)} = \min_{k \in [0, G-1]} W_{\text{dense}}[i, gG + k], \qquad w_{\max}^{(i,g)} = \max_{k \in [0, G-1]} W_{\text{dense}}[i, gG + k]$$

$$s^{(i,g)} = \max\left(\frac{w_{\max}^{(i,g)} - w_{\min}^{(i,g)}}{15.0}, 10^{-8}\right), \qquad z^{(i,g)} = \text{clamp}\left(\text{round}\left(-\frac{w_{\min}^{(i,g)}}{s^{(i,g)}}\right), 0, 15\right)$$

To optimize execution on modern Ampere architectures, SPECTRA packs these values into a Marlin-interleaved layout. Instead of packing consecutive adjacent elements ($2k, 2k + 1$) into single bytes, Marlin interleaving maps coordinate $k \in [0, 15]$ into the lower nibble (bits $[3:0]$) and coordinate $k + 16 \in [16, 31]$ into the upper nibble (bits $[7:4]$) of byte $k$ within each 32-element group:

Marlin Coordinate Nibble Interleaving

$$\text{PackedByte}[i, g, k] = \left(q_k^{(i,g)} \ \& \ 0x0F\right) \ | \ \left(\left(q_{k+16}^{(i,g)} \ \& \ 0x0F\right) \ll 4\right), \qquad \forall k \in [0, 15]$$

Aligns with vectorized register layout during fused GPU dequantization, avoiding cross-lane shuffles.

Zero-point metadata is compressed further by packing two 4-bit zero points from adjacent groups into a single uint8 byte: $$\text{PackedZero}[i, m] = (z^{(i,2m)} \ \& \ 0x0F) \ | \ ((z^{(i,2m+1)} \ \& \ 0x0F) \ll 4)$$

4.1 In-Register Fused W4A16 GEMV with Outlier Channel Accumulation (M = 1)

Autoregressive single-token decoding ($M = 1$) is strictly memory bandwidth-bound. 07. Architectural Discussion, Scope & Generality

7.1 Scope of Architecture Agnosticism

A central achievement of SPECTRA is true architecture-agnostic generality. Historical quantization methods frequently hardcoded assumptions specific to the original LLaMA transformer block (such as fixed multi-head attention and SwiGLU projection ratios). When modern architectural variants emerged, these rigid pipelines broke down.

SPECTRA operates at the abstract level of linear algebraic mappings preceded by normalization layers:

  • Dense Transformers (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B, Alibaba Qwen-3.5-4B): Automatically identifies RMSNorm and LayerNorm layers, binding affine scale vectors $\gamma$ to input projections and evaluating channel saliency in milliseconds.
  • Hybrid Convolutional State-Space Models (LiquidAI LFM-3-1.7B, LFM-2.5-2.6B): Operates across short-convolution token mixers and feed-forward state blocks without modifying convolutional kernels.
  • Hybrid Mamba-2 Architectures (IBM Granite-4.2-3B, NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Nano-4B): Seamlessly handles structured state-space layers, selective scan projections, and massive 131k-token embedding tables via dynamic row-gather dequantization.

7.2 The Hardware Pareto Frontier: Microscaling Group Size Dynamics

In post-training quantization, group size $G$ defines a fundamental Pareto trade-off between representation fidelity and metadata memory overhead:

  • Group-16 ($G = 16$): Yields an effective bit-rate of $5.25\text{ bpb}$. Scale and zero-point metadata consume $1.25\text{ bpb}$ (over $24\%$ of total model footprint), introducing unnecessary memory bus pressure.
  • Group-32 ($G = 32$): The optimal Pareto knee. Effective bit-rate is $4.625\text{ bpb}$ (metadata overhead is only $0.625\text{ bpb}$, or $13.5\%$). As proven in Proposition 3, local variance is bounded by $35.5\%$, completely eliminating outlier skew without sparse decomposition.
  • Group-64 and Group-128 ($G \ge 64$): Reduces metadata footprint ($4.31\text{ to }4.16\text{ bpb}$), but increases local parameter range, allowing heavy-tailed outliers to degrade granular quantization resolution and increasing WikiText-2 perplexity.

7.3 Edge Deployment Considerations: Thermals & Acoustic Profiles

Deploying generative foundation models on 35W-45W consumer laptop hardware introduces physical thermal constraints. Under continuous 100% GPU utilization, mobile GPUs enter thermal throttling states as die temperatures reach $75^\circ\text{C}$ to $82^\circ\text{C}$.

On Alibaba Qwen-3.5-4B, initial cold decoding runs at $14.55\text{ tok/s}$. Under sustained 10-minute generation runs, GPU clock frequencies throttle to maintain thermal equilibrium, stabilizing decoding at 12.08 tokens per second. Even under steady-state thermal throttling, SPECTRA sustains real-time conversational speeds (exceeding human reading speeds of 4-5 tok/s by more than 2.4x) within an acoustically quiet 35W power envelope.
